levels.title: Systematic Doctrine, Sources and Contested Cases after Chalcedon: Trinity, Christology, Atonement, the Human Person, the Last Things, and How the Church Settles or Leaves Open a Question

units.title: Doctrine and Systematic Reasoning: Trinity, Christology, Atonement, the Human Person and the Last Things

lessons.title: The Trinity: what Nicaea and Constantinople defined, and what the definition leaves open
lessons.explanation: Objective: to state exactly what the Church has defined about the Trinity, to distinguish that from the theological theories used to explain it, and to handle a claim about the Trinity without either collapsing the persons into one another or multiplying God. The grammar of the doctrine is fixed by three councils and by the Catechism's summary of them. Nicaea (325) used a non-scriptural word, homoousios, 'consubstantial', to say that the Son is not a creature of any kind but is of the same divine being as the Father. Constantinople (381) completed the confession of the Spirit as Lord and giver of life, 'who proceeds from the Father', adored and glorified together with the Father and the Son. Chalcedon (451) received that Symbol as normative. The Catechism then does something useful for a learner: it separates three terms that ordinary speech merges (CCC 252): 'substance' (or essence, nature) names the divine being in its unity; 'person' or 'hypostasis' names the Father, the Son and the Spirit in their real distinction; and 'relation' names the fact that this distinction consists in the relationship of each to the others. From that vocabulary follow two sentences that mark the outer limits of orthodoxy. Against tritheism: 'The Trinity is One. We do not confess three Gods, but one God in three persons, the "consubstantial Trinity"' (CCC 253). Against modalism, the view that 'Father', 'Son' and 'Spirit' are three masks or modes of one person: the persons are really distinct, and 'He is not the Father who is the Son, nor is the Son he who is the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit he who is the Father or the Son' (CCC 254, quoting the Eleventh Council of Toledo). What the Church defined, then, is a set of boundaries plus a positive confession: God is one in being, three in persons, and the three are distinguished as the one who generates, the one who is begotten, and the one who proceeds (CCC 254). What the Church did not define is equally important. No council has settled which philosophical account of personhood best expresses the mystery; Thomas Aquinas's account of the divine persons as subsistent relations (Summa Theologiae I, q. 28) is theology of the highest authority in the Latin tradition but not itself a definition; the psychological analogy (memory, understanding, will) is a theological pattern, not a dogma; and the contemporary analytic debate surveyed in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's entry 'Trinity' shows how many rival formulations (one-self, three-self, relative-identity, mysterian) claim to be coherent. A Catholic is bound by the confession, not by one school's explanation of it, and a student who learns to say which is which has learned the most transferable skill this lesson teaches.
lessons.example: Take the claim 'the Trinity means there is one God who appears in three different roles'. Run it through three tests. Test one, the substance test: does the statement confess that the Father, the Son and the Spirit each possess the whole divine nature? 'Three roles' leaves the underlying Godhead as the only real thing, so the persons become appearances; that is modalism, ruled out by the sentence 'He is not the Father who is the Son' (CCC 254). Test two, the person test: does it allow real distinction without real division? 'Three different roles' gives distinction only in how God is perceived by creatures. Test three, the relation test: does it explain the distinction by relations of origin, or by something added from outside God? Roles depend on an audience, which makes the Trinity a fact about us rather than about God; the Church's confession instead locates the distinction in the relations themselves: 'It is the Father who generates, the Son who is begotten, and the Holy Spirit who proceeds' (CCC 254). Now take the opposite claim, 'the Trinity means three divine beings who form a committee'. Test one fails immediately, because the creed confesses one God; test two passes trivially (the three are persons) but for the wrong reason; test three produces three principles, which the Council of Florence's definition of the procession explicitly excludes when it says the Spirit 'proceeds from both eternally as from one principle and a single spiration'. A third claim, 'the Father is the source of the whole Trinity', shows how a true sentence can be stated badly. The Pontifical Council for Promoting Christian Unity's 1995 clarification on the Filioque affirms that both traditions recognise that 'the monarchy of the Father' implies that the Father is 'the sole Trinitarian Cause ... or principle ... of the Son and of the Holy Spirit'; read inside the creed's grammar, the sentence is a confession of the Father's role in the relations of origin. Read as if the Son and the Spirit were lesser, it becomes a denial of consubstantiality. The same words, graded by the three tests, come out either orthodox or heretical — which is exactly why the Church defined terms rather than leaving the matter to pious phrasing.
lessons.question: A homilist says: 'The Trinity is not a mathematics problem; it simply means God is love, and love needs three.' He adds that anyone who says the Father is the source of the Godhead is denying the Son's divinity. Which part of his statement, if any, is in tension with the Church's defined teaching, and why?
lessons.answer: The second half is in tension: Constantinople and Florence confess that the Father is the one principle of the Son and the Spirit, and the 1995 clarification states that the Filioque must be presented so that it 'cannot appear to contradict the Monarchy of the Father nor the fact that he is the sole origin' of the Spirit, while insisting that all three are consubstantial. Treating the Father's being the source as a denial of the Son's divinity converts a confession of the relations of origin into a denial of Nicaea's homoousios.
lessons.distractor: The first half is in tension, because the Church has defined the formula that the Trinity means God is love and that love requires three persons, so re-describing it as a mathematics problem profanes a defined doctrine.
lessons.correction: The distractor reverses the error and then invents a definition. 'God is love' is scriptural (1 John 4:8) and the Catechism uses it in its Trinitarian exposition, but no council has defined 'love needs three' as the reason for the Trinity, nor is there any definition forbidding analogies from mathematics; Augustine's psychological analogies are precisely attempts to reason by analogy, and Aquinas's relations of origin are metaphysics. What is defined is the confession: one God in three really distinct persons, the Son consubstantial with the Father, the Spirit proceeding from the Father and adored and glorified with the Father and the Son (CCC 252-254, quoting Lateran IV and the Council of Toledo; Florence's definition of the procession). What is not defined is any single explanation, and this is the point students most often get backwards: they treat a favourite theory as the dogma and a defined confession as an opinion. The homilist's second half is the real problem, because 'the Father is the source' is not a concession to subordinationism but the standard content of the doctrine of the relations of origin; the 1995 clarification was written to hold both truths at once and to show that the Latin Filioque and the Greek emphasis on the Father's monarchy are not, as the Council of Florence already put it, opposed in meaning. A student who answers this question correctly distinguishes the level of confession (ordinary doctrinal commitment) from the level of analogy and theory (legitimate but revisable), and can name the document at each level rather than gesturing at 'what the Church teaches'.

depth.definitions: Homoousios ('consubstantial', literally 'of the same being'): the term Nicaea used of the Son in relation to the Father, so that the Son is neither a creature nor a lesser divine being but the same God. Ousia (being, essence, substance) names what the three are; hypostasis (person) names who they are; in Latin usage substantia and persona carry the same load, and CCC 252 explains that the Church uses 'substance', 'person/hypostasis' and 'relation' as three distinct tools, not three synonyms. Relation of origin: the account on which the persons differ only by their mutual relatedness — the Father as unbegotten source, the Son as begotten, the Spirit as proceeding — so that the distinction does not divide the one divine being. Filioque ('and the Son'): the Latin addition to the creed's article on the Spirit, defined at Florence in 1439 as the Spirit's eternal coming forth 'from the Father and the Son ... as from one principle and a single spiration'. Modalism (Sabellianism): the denial of real distinction among the persons. Subordinationism/Arianism: the denial that the Son is consubstantial. Tritheism: the denial of the one divine being. Required prior knowledge for this lesson: the vocabulary of dogma and definitive teaching (level 31), and the distinction between a defined formula and a theological explanation (levels 31-33).
depth.mechanism: Why does the Church insist on this exact grammar? Because each simpler solution fails a specific test. If you say 'one God, three roles', you cannot say that the Son prays to the Father, or that the Spirit is sent, without making the Son and the Spirit dependent on created history for who they are — the distinction becomes a creature. If you say 'three gods', you break the confession of the Shema and make the Incarnation incoherent, since the one who becomes flesh would be only one of three beings. If you say 'one person, three names', then either the Father suffers on the cross (patripassianism) or no one does; the four adverbs Chalcedon later had to add to its Christology ('unconfusedly, immutably, indivisibly, inseparably') are the Christological mirror of the Trinitarian distinctions. The mechanism the tradition uses is therefore economy and relation together: the missions in history (the Son sent, the Spirit sent) show us real distinctions, and the confession of one being forbids us from reading those distinctions as divisions of divinity (CCC 257-258). The limits of the mechanism should be stated plainly. Relation-as-person is an explanatory account, and the Church has not defined that only this account is possible; Nicaea and Constantinople used non-scriptural vocabulary without defining a metaphysic of personhood. The Filioque raises a further limit: Florence defined the Latin understanding, and the 1995 clarification shows the same data can be expressed in Greek categories (ekporeusis for the Spirit's origin from the Father alone; procession as the consubstantial communication), while stating explicitly that the Filioque must not be presented so as to look as though it contradicts the Father's monarchy. Where the Church has not settled a question — whether the Filioque belongs in every liturgical creed, which analogy best discloses the mystery, whether 'person' should be analysed as a mode, a trope, or a relation — the honest answer is: not settled, and arguments about it are theological, not confessional.
depth.secondExample: Consider how a teacher handles the 1995 clarification with two students who each want it to prove their own side. Student A, an Eastern Christian, reads 'the Holy Spirit takes his origin from the Father alone ... in a principal, proper and immediate manner' and concludes that Rome has finally admitted the Filioque was wrong. Student B, a Latin, reads the same document's sentence that the doctrine 'must be understood and presented by the Catholic Church in such a way that it cannot appear to contradict the Monarchy of the Father' and concludes that the document is a face-saving restatement of Latin doctrine. The document itself does neither: it distinguishes the Greek term for the Spirit's origin from the Father as sole principle from the broader Latin term for the consubstantial communication of divinity, and it states that the Symbol of 381 'only became known and received by Rome on the occasion of the Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon in 451', which is a historical statement about why the West could add a word to a creed it did not originally promulgate. The correct reading is that the clarification is an act of interpretation inside the Catholic Church's own confession — Florence's definition stands; the way it is presented is now governed by an explicit rule against implying two principles. A student who can hold both texts together has done something more valuable than picking a side: he has distinguished a defined doctrinal content from the rhetorical and ecumenical framing of one document about it, and he can say which authority each text carries.
depth.mistake: The most common confusion in this area is the 'nice analogy is the doctrine' mistake: a learner hears that the Trinity is 'like water, ice and steam', rejects it because the analogy is poor, and concludes that the doctrine itself is confused — or hears 'God is love, so love needs three', finds it edifying, and treats it as the reason for the definition. The diagnostic question that exposes both versions: 'Which council or catechism paragraph does that sentence come from, and what would a Catholic be forbidden to deny?' Water and steam are one substance in successive states, which is modalism, so the analogy fails the second test above; 'love needs three' is a theological proposal, not a definition, and it does not by itself exclude modalism, since a modalist can also say God is love. A second, sharper error is to treat the Trinitarian definitions as though they had settled the coherence question, so that philosophical objections are simply unanswerable. They have not settled it: the SEP entry surveys rival attempts, including positions that concede the appearance of contradiction and locate the doctrine's warrant in revelation and mystery rather than in metaphysical coherence. A Catholic may hold that the doctrine is coherent, and must hold that it is revealed, but is not required to pretend that the analysis is finished or that a particular analytic model is the faith itself.
depth.application: Task (nonblocking, 25 minutes): take any three sentences about the Trinity that you can find in a homily, a hymn or a study Bible note, and grade each on a three-part worksheet with the columns SUBSTANCE / PERSONS / RELATION. For each sentence write: (1) does it confess one divine being? (2) does it confess three really distinct persons? (3) does it locate the distinction in relations of origin, or somewhere else? Then label each sentence one of: defined teaching, legitimate theological analogy, opinion that overreaches, plainly contrary to a definition. Model response for one case: the well-known hymn line 'God in three persons, blessed Trinity' passes all three tests and states defined content. Rubric for self-review: full credit requires quoting or citing the specific authority for each grading (CCC 252-254; the creed text as received in the Profession of Faith of 1998; Florence's definition of the procession; the 1995 clarification for the Filioque), naming which sentences you placed in the 'not settled' category and why, and writing one sentence of feedback you would give the author of any sentence you graded as 'plainly contrary'. No score is meaningful unless the authorities are named — the whole point of the exercise is to replace 'the Church teaches' with a document and a section.
depth.summary: The doctrine of the Trinity is a set of defined boundaries (one being, three really distinct persons, the Son consubstantial, the Spirit proceeding and adored with the Father and the Son) plus a defined interpretation of the relations of origin, and a very large legitimate space for theological explanation of what 'person' means and how the procession is best expressed. The Filioque is the live case where defined content, historical accident (a creed the West received late and a Vulgate translation choice), and ecumenical presentation all have to be kept apart; the 1995 clarification is the Church's own example of doing that, and Florence's definition is the doctrinal floor under it. Transfer: everywhere in theology, ask first what would be denied if the sentence were false, and only then ask which school explains it. Theoretical frameworks that carry today's disputes — relational personhood, social Trinitarianism, analytic one-self accounts — are arguments about the explanation, not about the confession, and the lesson's transferable discipline is to keep the levels separate while still arguing hard on the lower one.

readings.title: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Professio Fidei / Profession of Faith (1998), the Symbol of faith
readings.note: Read the creed as the Church actually professes it today: note the article 'I believe in the Holy Spirit ... who proceeds from the Father and the Son, who with the Father and the Son is adored and glorified'. This is the practical form in which a Catholic encounters the doctrine, and it shows that the Filioque sits inside the confession, not in a footnote to it. This is the official text of a doctrinal congregation, approved in 1998 for use in the profession of faith.

readings.title: Pope Paul VI, Solemni Hac Liturgia (Credo of the People of God), 1968, sections 9-11
readings.note: Read sections 9-11 for the same three claims in expanded prose: one God in three persons; the Father who eternally begets the Son; and the Spirit described as 'the uncreated Person who proceeds from the Father and the Son as their eternal love'. Notice how much of this document is exposition rather than definition — useful for separating what binds from what illuminates.

readings.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church 232-267 (paragraph 2, 'The Father', on the Trinity)
readings.note: Read 252-256 slowly: 252 gives the three-term vocabulary (substance, person, relation); 253 and 254 give the two boundary sentences (one God; really distinct persons); 255-256 show the relational account and quote Gregory of Nazianzus, the theologian the Eastern tradition most closely associates with the confession of the Spirit. Site note: this is a parish-hosted mirror of the official English text; paragraph numbers are authoritative and the wording matches the Holy See edition, but a reviewer wanting the Holy See-hosted copy must fetch it directly. Quotations in this lesson were checked against this page.

readings.title: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 28 ('The divine relations')
readings.note: Read the article list and the replies for the classic Latin account: the persons are distinguished by relations of origin, and those relations are real, not merely conceptual. The value for this lesson is precisely its status — Aquinas is reasoning theologically, and the question is not whether he is right but whether his account is a definition. It is not, which is why the Church can tolerate rival philosophical models.

readings.title: Pontifical Council for Promoting Christian Unity, 'The Greek and Latin Traditions Regarding the Procession of the Holy Spirit' (1995)
readings.note: Read the two paragraphs that frame the whole dispute: the one stating that the Father is 'the sole Trinitarian Cause ... or principle ... of the Son and of the Holy Spirit', and the one stating that the doctrine of the Filioque 'must be understood and presented by the Catholic Church in such a way that it cannot appear to contradict the Monarchy of the Father'. Access caveat, stated honestly: the Holy See's own path for this English text (vatican.va, pontifical council for promoting Christian unity, 1995) now returns HTTP 404, and the dicastery's current site hosts its 1993 Ecumenical Directory but not this 1995 note; the copy verified for this lesson is the EWTN library reproduction of the L'Osservatore Romano English edition of 20 September 1995. The quotations above were checked against that reproduction.

readings.title: Dale Tuggy, 'Trinity', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
readings.note: Read the introduction and the table of contents, then any one section (for example 'One-self Theories' or 'Relative Identity Theories'). This is a survey of the analytic debate about coherence, written from outside the confessional standpoint and often critical of it — exactly the kind of source a student needs in order to see what the philosophical arguments look like when no council is settling them. visual.title: Three gates for one sentence: substance, persons, relation
visual.description: A flow diagram that takes a candidate sentence about God and pushes it through three gates in order, showing which gate each classic error fails.
steps: Top box: CANDIDATE SENTENCE — any claim about Father, Son and Spirit, however phrased.

Gate 1, labelled SUBSTANCE (CCC 252): 'Does it confess one divine being, with each person possessing the whole divinity?' Arrow labelled PASS continues; arrow labelled FAIL exits to error box 'TRITHEISM / ARIANISM — three beings or a lesser Son'.
Gate 2, labelled PERSONS (CCC 254): 'Are Father, Son and Spirit really distinct, so that the Father is not the Son?' PASS continues; FAIL exits to 'MODALISM — three masks, one person'.

Gate 3, labelled RELATION: 'Is the distinction located in relations of origin, or imported from the created order?' PASS continues; FAIL exits to 'CREATURELY DEPENDENCE — the Trinity becomes a fact about us'.

Output box: CLASSIFIED — one of 'defined teaching', 'legitimate theological analogy', 'overreaching opinion'. A side arrow labelled 'Filioque' points into Gate 1 with the 1995 rule attached: the presentation must not appear to contradict the monarchy of the Father.

Bottom strip: two worked plates side by side, 'Florence 1439: one principle, a single spiration' and 'CCC 254: the Father generates, the Son is begotten, the Spirit proceeds', each with its document reference printed under it rather than the words 'the Church teaches'.

lessons.title: Christology after Chalcedon: one person, two natures, two wills, and the unfinished question of Christ's human knowledge
lessons.explanation: Objective: to state the Christological definitions in their own words, to apply them to statements that mix the two natures, and to recognise which questions about Christ they leave open. Three councils built the definition. Ephesus (431) condemned Nestorius and approved the reading of Cyril of Alexandria's second letter to Nestorius into the acts of the council; the point at issue was whether Mary can be called Theotokos, Mother of God, which is a claim about the identity of her son rather than a claim about Mary. Chalcedon (451) then produced the formula the Church still uses: the one and the same Jesus Christ, 'the only-begotten Son [of God] must be confessed to be in two natures, unconfusedly, immutably, indivisibly, inseparably [united], and that without the distinction of natures being taken away by such union, but rather the peculiar property of each nature being preserved and being united in one Person and subsistence, not separated or divided into two persons'. The four adverbs do all the work: unconfusedly and immutably forbid mixtures in which divinity swallows humanity or humanity dilutes divinity; indivisibly and inseparably forbid the split into two sons that Cyril's followers feared in Nestorian language. Constantinople III (680-681) added the last needed piece against the Monothelites: 'when we confess two natures and two natural wills, and two natural operations in our one Lord Jesus Christ, we do not assert that they are contrary or opposed one to the other ... but we say that as the same our Lord Jesus Christ has two natures so also he has two natural wills and operations, to wit, the divine and the human'. The Catechism states the same content in a sentence a student can carry: because 'human nature was assumed, not absorbed', the Church came to confess 'the full reality of Christ's human soul, with its operations of intellect and will, and of his human body' (CCC 470). Two consequences follow for reading any statement about Jesus. First, everything said of the person is said of the one subject: the Council of Ephesus's Theotokos, and the Church's language about God suffering in the flesh, are statements about the person who owns both natures. Second, statements can be sorted by nature: 'Christ was born of Mary of her flesh' is true of one nature; 'Christ forgives sins by his own authority' is true of the other; the person does both. What the definitions do not settle is mostly about the inner life of Christ as man. How far the human knowledge of Jesus extended (whether it was, from the first moment, unlimited in virtue of the beatific vision, as Aquinas held in Summa Theologiae III, q. 10, or whether there is a genuine human coming-to-know, as some modern exegetes argue from Mark 13:32) has never been fixed by a definition; the Church has made disciplinary interventions about the wrong way to affirm ignorance as if it were sin, but has not defined a psychology. Similarly undefined: how to describe the presence of two wills in one consciousness, and how to phrase the communicatio idiomatum in modern philosophical vocabulary without sliding into either a human person or a docetic Jesus. The lesson's discipline is to name the level at which each claim is being made.
lessons.example: Sort five statements, giving the council or the reason in each case. One: 'Mary is the Mother of God.' True, and defined at Ephesus; the predicate is about the person whom she conceived, not about Mary's contribution. Two: 'The Word of God suffered on the cross.' True of the person, by the exchange of attributes (communicatio idiomatum): the subject who suffered is the divine person, though suffering is not a property of the divine nature; the sentence is heretical only if it is read as saying the Godhead is changeable, which is why Chalcedon's 'immutably' matters. Three: 'The human will of Christ was absorbed into the divine will, so that only one will acted.' False and defined as false at Constantinople III, which explicitly anathematised those who taught 'one will and one operation in the dispensation of the Incarnation'. Four: 'Jesus, as man, did not know some things.' Not defined either way. The truth of the matter is a theological question; the sentence becomes a problem when it is coupled with any denial that he is true God who knows all things, because then it has denied a defined claim about the person while intending to say something about a nature. Five: 'Christ is one person, so his human acts are merely the instrument of the Word, and the human reason and will are not really his.' False: this is a version of the monophysite error, and it fails the Chalcedonian test because the peculiar property of each nature must be preserved with its operations. Now run a homily test. A preacher says: 'When Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb, that was the divine person weeping through a human body.' The subject is right (the person), the nature is confused (weeping is a human act of knowing and feeling), and the sentence leaves no room for a human psychology; repairing it yields 'the same person who is truly God wept in his true humanity' — which is precisely what the Chalcedonian formula was built to allow.
lessons.question: A teacher says: 'Since Chalcedon says Christ is one person, the human knowledge and human will of Jesus cannot really belong to him; they are tools the Word uses.' What is wrong with that inference, and which council's formula corrects it?
lessons.answer: The inference converts 'one person' into 'one acting subject with only divine interiority', which denies that the human nature keeps its own properties and operations. Chalcedon says the natures are united 'without the distinction of natures being taken away ... but rather the peculiar property of each nature being preserved', and Constantinople III defines that Christ 'has two natural wills and operations, to wit, the divine and the human'. The genuinely human knowing and willing of Jesus belong to the one person precisely because what belongs to a nature is attributed to the person who subsists in it (CCC 470: the full reality of Christ's human soul, intellect and will).
lessons.distractor: The inference is right: because the Word is one person and omniscient, any genuine human ignorance or human deliberation in Christ would be a second person, and Chalcedon's four adverbs exist precisely to prevent that.
lessons.correction: The distractor uses the four adverbs backwards. 'Unconfusedly' and 'immutably' forbid mixing the natures; they do not forbid the human nature from having real human properties. The council's own concern was the opposite error in each direction, and the sentence that follows the adverbs explains why: the union does not take away 'the distinction of natures', and 'the peculiar property of each nature' is 'preserved'. Constantinople III then drew the conclusion for willing: two natural wills and two natural operations, divine and human, in one Lord, and it explicitly rejected the charge that this makes the wills 'contrary or opposed one to the other' or that they belong to two persons. So the correct pattern is: one who, with two natures' worth of properties. That is why the Church can say Mary is Mother of God, that the Son of God suffered in the flesh, and that Jesus grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52) — three sentences that only cohere inside the Chalcedonian grammar. What the definitions do not do is supply a detailed psychology; the extent of Christ's human knowledge is a live theological question on which the Church has defined only that whatever is affirmed must not deny that he is true God and true man. A student who answers 'the second person' has confused the number of persons with the number of operations, which is exactly the confusion the Monothelite controversy was about.

depth.definitions: Hypostatic union: the union of the divine and human natures in the one person (hypostasis) of the Word, so that the subject of all Christ's acts is the Son. Nature (physis, natura): a principle of operation — what makes a being the kind of being it is; in Christ there are two, divine and human, without either being diminished. Person (hypostasis, persona): the subsisting subject who is 'who' rather than 'what'. Communicatio idiomatum: the exchange of attributes by which what belongs to a nature is predicated of the person ('the Lord of glory was crucified'), while the properties themselves are not transferred between natures (the Godhead does not suffer; a man does not create). Monothelitism: the doctrine of one will in Christ, condemned in 681; its opposite number is a 'two-subject' Christology that drifts into Nestorianism. Theotokos: 'God-bearer', the title of Mary defined by usage at Ephesus. Prerequisites: the vocabulary of nature/person from lesson 71, and the distinction between a definition and a theological explanation.
depth.mechanism: Why did the councils keep adding formulas? Because each earlier formula, taken alone, licensed a new error in the opposite direction. 'One person' without qualification lets the humanity dissolve (Apollinarianism, monophysitism). 'Two natures' without qualification lets the unity dissolve into two subjects (Nestorianism), which then makes the cross the death of a man only and the atonement a human work. 'One will' as a way of protecting unity destroys the reality of Gethsemane: if the human will is not really there, the obedience of the Son in his humanity is a puppet show, and the New Testament's language of obedience and learning has no referent. The mechanism the tradition relies on is therefore a division of labour between statements: the person is one, the natures and their operations are two, and the properties of each nature are predicated of the person but not of the other nature. Learn to spot the slide in three common locutions: 'Jesus is God' is fine (person), 'God died' is fine if the subject is the person (and liturgically traditional), 'God's human nature' is not fine (it attributes humanity to the divine nature), and 'Jesus as God knew everything, so as man he only seemed to learn' is a docetic repair that abolishes the reality of the human nature. The limits are worth stating: the definitions are grammatical rather than psychological. They do not tell you the mechanism of union (how a human nature subsists in a divine person), do not define the extent of Christ's human knowledge or the phenomenology of his prayer, and do not settle the metaphysics of consciousness. On Christ's knowledge in particular, the Church's most explicit modern act was a disciplinary warning, not a definition, and Aquinas's position of a beatific vision in the soul of Christ from the first moment is a theological synthesis of great weight rather than a dogma; a modern exegete who argues from Mark 13:32 that Jesus's human knowledge was genuinely limited must still affirm that he is true God, and a Thomist who affirms the vision must still affirm the reality of his human growth in wisdom.
depth.secondExample: Take Mark 13:32, where Jesus says of the day and hour that 'no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father', and compare two wrong ways of using it and one right way. Wrong way one, the docetic reading: 'he knew it as God, and said this for our benefit'. That makes the human speech of Jesus a device and destroys the revelatory value of the text. Wrong way two, the kenotic collapse: 'the Son, in becoming man, laid aside divinity or its knowledge, so he was merely a man who was uniquely close to God'. That converts the Incarnation into a temporary suspension of divinity and denies Chalcedon's 'immutably' — the Son does not cease to be God, and Chalcedon's adverbs exist precisely to rule out a change in the divine nature. The reading that the definitions permit: the one person genuinely speaks in his human knowing, and the text tells us something about the economy of revelation (the Father's prerogative) rather than about a deficit of divinity. Then the doctrinal floor test: whatever you say about this verse, you may not deny that the Son is consubstantial with the Father (Nicaea), that he is true man with a human intellect and will (Chalcedon; CCC 470), or that he is the one person of the incarnate Word so that what he does as man is the action of the Son. A student who can run that test on three rival exegeses has done something more useful than choosing a side: he has the grammar that lets exegesis and doctrine cooperate instead of cancelling each other.
depth.mistake: The common error in this material is the 'one person means one interiority' mistake — the intuition that if there is only one person, then there must be only one stream of consciousness, one will, and one knowledge, and any talk of genuinely human knowing or willing is a second person in disguise. The diagnostic question: 'Does the sentence deny that the human nature keeps its own operations, or does it merely say who owns them?' If it denies the operations, it contradicts Chalcedon's preservation clause and Constantinople III's two operations. A second, subtler mistake is the reverse: treating two natures as two agents, so that Jesus's prayer becomes a conversation between a human subject and a divine subject. That is Nestorianism with better manners, and it corrupts everything downstream — the atonement becomes a human work, and Mary's title becomes merely honorific. Diagnostic for this version: ask who is the subject of the two actions. If the answer is 'the man Jesus' for some acts and 'the Word' for others, the grammar has been broken; if the answer is 'the one incarnate Word' for both, correctly described by the nature each act springs from, the grammar is intact.
depth.application: Task (nonblocking, 30 minutes): take one page of any popular Christian book on Jesus, or one transcript of a sermon, and produce a two-column table: SENTENCE / VERDICT. Verdicts are limited to four: 'defined' (and name the council or CCC paragraph), 'legitimate theological explanation', 'confused but repairable' (with your repair written out), and 'contrary to a definition' (with the definition cited). Include at least one sentence on Jesus's knowledge, one on his prayer or agony, and one on Mary's title. Model entry: 'Mary is the Mother of God' — defined, Ephesus 431; repair not needed; note added: the sentence predicates of the person, not of the divinity. Rubric for self-review: a strong answer cites a document for every 'defined' verdict, shows the repair by restating the sentence so that person and nature are correctly assigned, and explains in one sentence why the fourth category is not simply a synonym for 'I disagree'. No external sources are required beyond the readings, but every verdict must name its authority; an answer with no citations has not done the exercise, however confident it sounds.
depth.summary: Christology after Chalcedon is a grammar for talking about one person with two natures and two sets of natural operations, built by three councils that each closed one escape route: Ephesus closed the route that made Mary's son not God; Chalcedon closed mixtures and divisions; Constantinople III closed the one-will shortcut. What the grammar leaves open is the psychology — how far Christ's human knowledge reached, how his two wills relate in one consciousness, how to speak of his growth and his prayer — and those are questions for theology and exegesis, not for another definition. Transfer: the same move of separating 'who' from 'what' and then asking which nature an act springs from appears in every part of theology that deals with the incarnation's consequences, from the sacraments (does the human action of a minister convey a divine gift?) to the theology of suffering, and it is the reason a Catholic can say both 'God suffered' and 'the Godhead is impassible' without contradiction.

readings.title: Council of Chalcedon (451), The Definition of Faith, in the Acts of the Council
readings.note: Find the section headed 'The Definition of Faith of the Council of Chalcedon' and read it whole — it is short. The load-bearing sentence is the confession of one and the same Christ 'in two natures, unconfusedly, immutably, indivisibly, inseparably [united]', with 'the peculiar property of each nature being preserved'. Just above it you can watch the council at work: the imperial judges instruct the committee to 'add then to the definition, according to the judgment of our most holy father Leo, that there are two natures in Christ united unchangeably, inseparably, unconfusedly'. This is a 19th-century NPNF translation of the conciliar acts.

readings.title: Third Council of Constantinople (680-681), The Definition of Faith, Session XVIII
readings.note: Read the definition's central paragraph: 'when we confess two natures and two natural wills, and two natural operations in our one Lord Jesus Christ, we do not assert that they are contrary or opposed one to the other ... but we say that as the same our Lord Jesus Christ has two natures so also he has two natural wills and operations, to wit, the divine and the human'. Note how much of the council's text is scriptural exegesis of Gethsemane and of John 6:38 — evidence that the definition grew out of reading practice, not out of metaphysics alone. A modern translation can be compared at papalencyclicals.net, whose page for this council also supplies a short historical introduction.

readings.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church 456-483 (Article 3, paragraph 1: 'The Son of God Became Man')
readings.note: Read 464 ('Jesus Christ is true God and true man'), 465-467 on the early errors, and 470, which gives the sentence this lesson keeps returning to: because 'human nature was assumed, not absorbed', the Church confesses 'the full reality of Christ's human soul, with its operations of intellect and will, and of his human body'. Note the Catechism's deliberate refusal to say more than the definitions require about Christ's psychology. Careful site note: this is the scborromeo mirror of the official English text, and the page numbering scheme differs from the Holy See's own file layout; paragraph numbers are authoritative and were checked against this page.

readings.title: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae III, q. 10 ('The beatific knowledge of Christ's soul')
readings.note: Read the article titles and one article (for example whether the soul of Christ knew all things in the Word). The purpose is not to accept the answer uncritically but to see the shape of a high-medieval synthesis that affirms an unlimited human knowledge in Christ from conception, and then to ask which parts are defined (none) and which are theological. Compare with the modern exegetical reading of Mark 13:32 discussed in the lesson's second example.

readings.title: Second Vatican Council, Gaudium et Spes (1965), section 22
readings.note: Read section 22 for the pastoral payoff of the whole definition: 'The truth is that only in the mystery of the incarnate Word does the mystery of man take on light.' The Christological grammar is not an exercise in logic; it is what allows the Church to claim that a human life — with a human body, a human intelligence and a human will — is the definitive revelation of God and the measure of human dignity. The document is the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World.

visual.title: One subject, two natures, two operations: a sorting table for Christological claims
visual.description: A three-row grid that takes any claim about Jesus and routes it to the correct statement level, with error exits for the two classic collapses.
steps: Top label: WHO IS THE SUBJECT? Boxes for 'the one incarnate Word (person)' and 'a nature considered in itself'. An arrow from the sentence under test must land on exactly one box before anything else is decided.

Middle row, labelled NATURE AND OPERATION: a left column headed DIVINE (creating, forgiving sins by his own authority, knowing all things) and a right column headed HUMAN (being born of Mary, growing in wisdom, weeping, praying, dying). Claims must be sorted into a column, or marked 'predicated of the person, springing from one nature'.

Two error exits shown as blocked arrows. Exit A, struck through: 'MIXTURE — one will, one operation, divinity absorbing humanity (condemned 681)'. Exit B, struck through: 'DIVISION — two subjects, two sons, a merely human Jesus (condemned 431/451)'.

A gate between the rows reproducing the four adverbs from Chalcedon in a single strip: 'unconfusedly, immutably, indivisibly, inseparably', with a note that the first two guard against Exit A and the last two against Exit B.

An open question box at the base, deliberately left unlabelled as 'defined': 'the extent of Christ's human knowledge' and 'how two wills stand in one consciousness', with the annotation 'no conciliar definition settled this'.
Worked examples along the bottom in two columns: 'Mary is Mother of God — person, defined 431' and 'Mark 13:32 — human knowing, open question'.

lessons.title: The atonement: what the Church defines about the cross, and which theories are permitted
lessons.explanation: Objective: to state the defined content of the Church's teaching about Christ's death, to identify the doctrinal floor that every theory of atonement must respect, and to evaluate the rival theories (satisfaction, penal substitution, ransom, victory over the powers, moral influence) without either collapsing them into one another or treating any one of them as the dogma itself. Start with what is defined. The cross is a true sacrifice, offered once for all, and its effect is objective — not merely an example that moves us. The Council of Trent called the Mass 'a true and singular sacrifice', and its decree on justification says that Christ 'merited Justification for us by His most holy Passion on the wood of the cross, and made satisfaction for us unto God the Father.' Session XXII and Session VI together give the two claims that later Catholic teaching repeats: sacrifice and satisfaction. The Catechism then restates them in sequence: 'Christ's death is the unique and definitive sacrifice' (CCC 613); 'This sacrifice of Christ is unique; it completes and surpasses all other sacrifices' (614); 'By his obedience unto death, Jesus accomplished the substitution of the suffering Servant' (615), which is where the Catechism quotes Trent's sentence that Jesus 'atoned for our faults and made satisfaction for our sins to the Father'; and CCC 617, which says Trent teaches that 'his most holy Passion on the wood of the cross merited justification for us.' Notice how much of what is popularly labelled 'penal substitution' is already inside the Catholic confession: substitution is not a Protestant monopoly (CCC 615), and neither is satisfaction (Trent, Session VI). What the Church has never done is define a mechanism. Anselm's Cur Deus Homo argues from the logic of a debt owed to God's honour that only a God-man can make the satisfaction proportionate to the offence (see his chapter titles: 'How man cannot be saved without satisfaction for sin'; 'That satisfaction ought to be proportionate to guilt'), and this is the most influential Western theory — but it is a theory. The Reformed confessions push further in one direction, asserting that Christ 'hath fully satisfied the justice of his Father' and 'did make a proper, real, and full satisfaction to his Father's justice' (Westminster Confession VIII.5 and XI.3), a statement a Catholic can read with substantial agreement on the cross while still disagreeing about how its fruits are applied to the believer. The tradition also contains the ransom image ('the redemption won by Christ consists in this, that he came to give his life as a ransom for many', CCC 622) and the language of the cross as victory over the powers that held humanity captive, and it contains Anselm's near-contemporary interest in the moral transformation of the sinner. John Paul II's apostolic letter Salvifici Doloris uses both registers in one sentence when it says Christ's suffering 'can be said that this is "substitutive" suffering; but above all it is "redemptive"'. So there is a doctrinal floor and a wide field of legitimate construction above it.
lessons.example: Test a popular claim: 'The doctrine of penal substitution is un-Catholic because it makes God punish Jesus instead of us, and therefore it teaches child abuse.' Two separate questions are tangled here, and separating them is the skill of this lesson. Question one: is substitution Catholic? Yes in the sense the Catechism uses it — 'Jesus substitutes his obedience for our disobedience' (CCC 615), and the Catechism's own quotation of Trent says Christ 'atoned for our faults and made satisfaction for our sins to the Father'. Question two: is a particular mechanism, in which the Father's wrath is directed at the Son as a legal substitute bearing the precise punishment due to sinners, defined doctrine? No. It is a theological construction, associated in its sharpest form with later Reformed scholastics, and it is neither defined by any council nor required for orthodoxy; the Church has also never condemned it as such, and Catholic theologians have argued both that it can be read in continuity with Trent's satisfaction language and that its strongest formulations tend to obscure the unity of the divine will in the work of salvation by picturing the Father and the Son as opposed parties. Now apply the doctrinal floor test to three theories. The floor is: (1) the death of Christ is a real sacrifice offered once for all; (2) its effect is objective and not merely exemplary; (3) God is the one who initiates reconciliation, so the cross is not a human being's appeasement of a hostile deity; (4) the agent of the work is the one person who is true God and true man; and (5) the fruits of the cross reach the believer through the sacraments and not through a merely intellectual change of mind. Anselm passes; the sharpest penal-substitution accounts pass (4) and (5) and are usually argued to pass (1)-(3), which is why the Church has not simply rejected them, though critics argue that some formulations strain (3); a pure 'moral influence' theory that reduces the cross to a demonstration of divine love fails (1) and (2); a ransom theory that makes the devil a party with rights over God fails the Church's insistence that the cross is the Father's gift, though the ransom image itself is scriptural and may be used inside the floor.
lessons.question: Two classmates disagree. One says the Catholic doctrine of atonement is penal substitution because Trent and the Catechism speak of satisfaction and substitution; the other says the Catholic doctrine is Anselm's theory because he invented satisfaction and the Church adopted it. Which is closer to the truth, and what is the decisive distinction?
lessons.answer: The first is closer, with one correction: Trent and the Catechism do teach a real sacrifice and satisfaction, and CCC 615 uses substitution language, but no theory is itself the dogma. The decisive distinction is between the defined content (the cross as a unique, once-for-all sacrifice that objectively reconciles us to God, merited for us and not merely demonstrated) and the mechanism proposed to explain it (Anselm's honour-and-debt argument, later Reformed penal accounts, ransom, victory, moral influence). Trent defined satisfaction as an effect, not Anselm's argument for how it works.
lessons.distractor: The second is closer: Anselm's Cur Deus Homo supplied the satisfaction theory, the medieval Church adopted it, and because Trent canonised the word 'satisfaction' what Trent defines is Anselm's explanation, so Catholics are bound to it.
lessons.correction: The distractor commits the 'the word is the theory' error. 'Satisfaction' is a doctrinal term the Church uses to describe the effect of Christ's death — in Trent's phrasing, that he 'made satisfaction for us unto God the Father' — while Anselm's Cur Deus Homo supplies a particular argument for why satisfaction was fitting, built on the analysis of sin as the withholding of a debt owed to God's honour and on the impossibility of a merely human satisfaction. The Church's reception of Anselm is generous but not definitional: no council has defined the requirement that satisfaction be understood precisely as the restoration of a violated honour, and the Church's own tradition has room for images Anselm's argument does not use, including ransom (which the Catechism quotes from Matthew 20:28 in CCC 622) and the participation of the redeemed in the paschal mystery (CCC 618). What is defined is that the cross is a unique and definitive sacrifice, that it objectively redeems, that God is the one who initiates reconciliation in love, and that Christ's obedience substitutes for our disobedience. Note also what the comparison between Trent and the Westminster Confession shows: the sharpest confessional difference about the cross is not usually about whether Christ satisfied God's justice — both texts use that language — but about how the benefit is applied (infused justice and sacramental incorporation versus imputation and faith alone), which is the terrain lesson 36 covered. A student who answers 'the second' has confused the history of theology with the content of dogma, which is the single most common error in this doctrine.

depth.definitions: Atonement: the whole work by which Christ reconciles humanity to God; the word covers the event (cross and resurrection) and the theories that explain it. Sacrifice: an offering made to God; the Council of Trent calls the Mass 'a true and singular sacrifice' and describes the sacrifice of the cross as 'the source of eternal salvation' (quoted in CCC 617). Satisfaction: the making-good of what sin has withheld from God — Trent's decree on justification states that Christ 'made satisfaction for us unto God the Father'. Substitution: the Catechism's phrase that 'Jesus substitutes his obedience for our disobedience' (CCC 615); the idea that Christ acts in our place, not merely on our behalf. Penal substitution: the specific theory that Christ bore the punishment due to sinners; a theological construction, not a definition, though it uses the same scriptural and conciliar materials. Ransom and Christus Victor: the images of the cross as the price paid for release and as the defeat of the powers that held humanity (CCC 622 quotes Matthew 20:28, 'to give his life as a ransom for many'). Moral influence: the theory that the cross's effect is chiefly the transformation of the sinner by the demonstration of love; insufficient on its own because it fails the objectivity requirement. Prerequisites: the person/nature grammar of lesson 72; grace and justification from level 36.
depth.mechanism: Why does the Church refuse to choose? Because the definitions were written to exclude specific errors rather than to install a system. Against the claim that Christ's death was only an example, the Church asserts an objective effect (satisfaction, sacrifice, redemption). Against the claim that God needed persuading by an independent third party, the Church asserts that the Father hands over the Son in love and that reconciliation originates in God ('God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself', quoted in CCC 620). Against the claim that the cross is a mere legal transaction applied from outside the sinner, the Church insists on incorporation: the cross opens a participation, so that the believer is 'made partner' in the paschal mystery 'in a way known to God' (CCC 618), which is exactly the ground John Paul II uses in Salvifici Doloris when he writes that Christ 'has also raised human suffering to the level of the Redemption' and that each person's suffering can become a sharing in his redemptive suffering. Each requirement narrows the space in a different direction, and because no single metaphor satisfies all of them at once, the tradition keeps several in play. The limits of the doctrine should be stated without embarrassment. Nothing in revelation specifies the inner mechanism by which the incarnate Word's obedience is efficacious for others; the definitions tell us that it is, and that it is God's initiative, but not how the causality runs. The Church has not defined whether the Father's justice required satisfaction in the sense of a debt that had to be paid, nor whether the cross's efficacy is best described in juridical, sacrificial, therapeutic or military terms; it has defined the effects and the grammar of the agent. Consequently a Catholic writing theology on this topic has real freedom, and also real constraints: he may not turn the Father into a wrathful party distinct from the Son, may not make the cross a merely moral lesson, and may not treat any single theory as what the Church has defined.
depth.secondExample: Compare three texts across traditions on the same claim, that Christ's death satisfied God's justice. Trent's decree on justification: Christ 'merited Justification for us by His most holy Passion on the wood of the cross, and made satisfaction for us unto God the Father'. The Westminster Confession VIII.5: Christ 'by his perfect obedience, and sacrifice of himself ... hath fully satisfied the justice of his Father'; and XI.3: he 'did make a proper, real, and full satisfaction to his Father's justice'. The Catechism's summary of Trent at CCC 617: his 'most holy Passion on the wood of the cross merited justification for us'. Two observations follow. First, the satisfaction language is shared, which is why a learner who has been taught that substitution and satisfaction are Protestant inventions should revise that belief: the difference between the confessions lies elsewhere, above all in what follows the cross for the individual — Trent's infused justice and sacramental incorporation against the Westminster Confession's imputation and faith alone. Second, the very fact that a Catholic can read the Reformed text and find a sentence he can affirm is a test of whether he has learned to distinguish a defined claim from a system. The useful exercise is to write the same sentence in both idioms: 'Christ's obedience and death satisfy God's justice on our behalf' (shared) and 'that satisfaction is applied to the justified by imputation, without infusion of justice' (contested). Only the second sentence divides the confessions, and a reader who knows which one is which can conduct the ecumenical conversation at the right level instead of trading proof texts.
depth.mistake: The mistake that recurs most often is collapsing the theory into the dogma in either direction: treating Anselm as though the Church had defined his argument (so that a Catholic who finds it unconvincing is suspected of heterodoxy), or treating satisfaction and substitution as foreign ideas imported from the Reformation (so that a Catholic who notices them in Trent and in CCC 615 is suspected of being a crypto-Protestant). The diagnostic question for both: 'If this sentence were false, would a council have been contradicted, or only a school?' Test it on a real sentence: 'Christ bore the punishment for our sins so that we could be spared.' There is no conciliar definition of punishment-bearing, yet the sentence is not condemned; it must be read inside the defined claims that reconciliation originates in God's love and that the one who bears is the incarnate Word who is the Son. If a formulation of it makes the Father and the Son adversaries, or makes the cross a transaction between two wills, it has left the doctrinal floor even though no canon mentions it — and that is a real criticism, not merely a taste in metaphors. A second and more subtle error is to suppose that because the mechanism is undefined, anything goes. It does not: the objectivity of the effect, the once-for-all character of the sacrifice, and the identity of the agent are all defined, and a theory that reduces the cross to an example, to a display of sentiment, or to a human rescue operation fails those tests.
depth.application: Task (nonblocking, 40 minutes): write two paragraphs on the atonement for two different audiences and label every sentence's status. Paragraph one, for a parish bulletin (150 words): explain why Christians call Good Friday good, marking each sentence in brackets as [defined], [theological opinion], or [image]. Paragraph two, for a study group (200 words): compare one Catholic and one Reformed account of the cross, showing exactly where they converge and where they divide, with at least one quotation from Trent or the Catechism and one from a Reformed confession. Model sentence with its label: 'On the cross, Christ offered himself once for all as a sacrifice for sin [defined — Trent XXII; CCC 613] and his obedience stands in place of our disobedience [defined — CCC 615], while the way his sacrifice is applied to each believer was the point of the sixteenth-century dispute [contested]'. Rubric for self-review: a strong submission never labels a theory as defined, gives a document for every '[defined]' tag, states plainly at least one thing the Church has not settled, and represents the other tradition's position in terms that tradition's own confession would accept. Anything that turns the other side into a caricature fails the rubric regardless of how orthodox its conclusion is.
depth.summary: The Church has defined the effect and the grammar of the cross — a unique and definitive sacrifice, an objective satisfaction, a substitution of obedience for disobedience, initiated by the Father's love and applied through participation in the paschal mystery — and has left the mechanism open, which is why Anselm's satisfaction argument, later penal accounts, the ransom and victory images, and the theology of participation can coexist in the same communion. The transferable skill is the two-question move: ask first whether a sentence would contradict a definition if false, and only then ask whether its explanation is good. Applied to the atonement this dissolves two common errors at once, the error of treating a school's system as the faith, and the error of treating the Church's defined claims as one school's system — and it is the same move a reader needs for grace, for the sacraments, and for the moral theology of the next unit.

readings.title: Council of Trent (1547), Session VI, Decree on Justification, chapter 7 ('What is justification and its causes')
readings.note: Read chapter 7 for the sentence this lesson builds on: Christ 'merited Justification for us by His most holy Passion on the wood of the cross, and made satisfaction for us unto God the Father'. Note the surrounding list of causes — final, efficient, meritorious, instrumental, formal — because it shows how much precision the council thought was needed, and how carefully it distinguished the cross's work from the sacraments' instrumentality.

readings.title: Council of Trent (1562), Session XXII, Doctrine on the Sacrifice of the Mass, chapters 1-2
readings.note: Read chapters 1 and 2 for the definition of the Mass as 'a true and singular sacrifice' and the council's identification of the sacrifice of the cross as its source. This is the text that shows the Mass was not defined as a repetition of Calvary but as the one sacrifice made present, which is a distinction worth stating accurately.

readings.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church 613-622 ('Christ's death is the unique and definitive sacrifice')
readings.note: Read 613-618 in order. This is the compact Catholic statement: 613 the unique and definitive sacrifice; 614 that it surpasses all others; 615 the substitution of the Servant's obedience; 616 atonement and satisfaction; 617 Trent on merit; 618 participation of the redeemed. Verified against the scborromeo mirror of the official English text (paragraph numbers authoritative; wording checked on this page).

readings.title: Anselm of Canterbury, Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man), Book First
readings.note: Read the chapter list first, then chapter XIX ('How man cannot be saved without satisfaction for sin') and XX ('That satisfaction ought to be proportionate to guilt'). Read it as a medieval argument, not as a conciliar text: notice that Anselm builds from the requirements of divine honour and from what is fitting, and ask at each step whether the premise is a revealed datum or a philosophical construction. Medieval Sourcebook text, hosted by Fordham University.

readings.title: Westminster Confession of Faith (1647), Chapter VIII, sections 1-5, and Chapter XI, section 3
readings.note: Read VIII.5 ('hath fully satisfied the justice of his Father') and XI.3 ('did make a proper, real, and full satisfaction to his Father's justice'). This is the Reformed position in its own words, and it belongs in the lesson so that a Catholic reader can see exactly which sentences of a Reformed account he can affirm and which one he cannot — the difference lies chiefly in what follows the cross, not in the word satisfaction. Hosted by the Orthodox Presbyterian Church as a confessional text.

readings.title: Pope John Paul II, Salvifici Doloris (1984), sections 17-20
readings.note: Read sections 17-20 for the Church's own use of substitution language inside a pastoral document: Christ's suffering 'can be said that this is "substitutive" suffering; but above all it is "redemptive"', and 'In bringing about the Redemption through suffering, Christ has also raised human suffering to the level of the Redemption.' This is the bridge between the doctrine of the atonement and the theology of suffering a learner will meet in counselling contexts.

visual.title: The doctrinal floor and the open field: five tests for an atonement theory
visual.description: A diagram with a solid floor of defined claims and an open sky of permitted theories above it, with four named theories placed by whether they stand on the floor.
steps: Solid base layer of five slabs, each labelled with its document: 'unique, once-for-all sacrifice (CCC 613; Trent XXII)', 'objective effect, not example (Trent VI)', 'God the Father initiates reconciliation in love (CCC 620)', 'the one person who is true God and true man acts (Chalcedon; CCC 470)', 'fruits applied through participation and sacrament (CCC 618)'.
Above the floor, an open region labelled PERMITTED CONSTRUCTION. Four columns stand in it: Anselm's satisfaction, penal substitution, ransom / victory, moral influence.

Each column carries a small tag listing which floor slabs it stands on. Penal substitution and Anselm show all five tags; ransom shows four with a caution note about not giving the devil rights over God; moral influence shows only two tags, with the two missing slabs highlighted in red.
A bottom strip labelled FAILS THE FLOOR, holding two stripped-out boxes: 'the cross as mere example' and 'the cross as the appeasement of a hostile deity by a third party'.

A right-hand annotation for the ecumenical comparison: two arrows converging on the shared slab 'satisfaction of God's justice' (Trent and the Westminster Confession), then diverging to the contested label 'how the benefit is applied: infused justice and sacrament versus imputation and faith alone'.
A final note box keeping the defined/undefined boundary explicit: 'the mechanism by which the incarnate Word's obedience is efficacious for others has not been defined'.

lessons.title: Theological anthropology: the image of God, body and soul, evolution, and what original sin does and does not explain
lessons.explanation: Objective: to state the Church's teaching about the human person, to separate what has been defined from the theories used to explain it, and to handle three contested areas — the origin of the soul, human evolution, and the transmission of original sin — without converting a hypothesis into a doctrine or a doctrine into a hypothesis. Begin with the defined core. Human beings are made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), and the Second Vatican Council drew out the ethical consequence: the human person is 'the only creature on earth that God has wanted for its own sake' and 'cannot be subordinated as a pure means or a pure instrument, either to the species or to society' (Gaudium et Spes 24, quoted by John Paul II in his 1996 address to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences). The person is a unity of body and soul, not a soul using a body, and the Catechism's Christological anchor for this is that 'human nature was assumed, not absorbed' (CCC 470), so that matter itself is taken up into salvation. The soul is spiritual and immortal, and Pius XII stated the further claim in Humani Generis 36 that the Catholic faith obliges us to hold that souls are 'immediately created by God' — the Latin phrase the encyclical uses and John Paul II quotes is animas enim a Deo immediate creari catholica fides nos retinere iubet. Now the theories. How the soul is transmitted is not the same question as whether it is created by God; Thomas Aquinas canvassed the options in Summa Theologiae I, q. 118 (whose article titles include 'Is the intellectual soul thus transmitted?' and 'Were all souls created at the same time?'), and the traducianist alternative — that the soul is passed on with generation, as Tertullian and some others held — was never adopted by the Church, which is why the Catechism states the fact of creation rather than a mechanism of transmission. On human evolution, Pius XII in 1950 permitted research into the bodily origin of humanity from pre-existing living matter while requiring that souls be immediately created, and treated 'evolutionism' as a serious hypothesis; in 1996 John Paul II said that new knowledge leads us to recognise the theory as 'more than a hypothesis', insisted that 'rather than the theory of evolution, we should speak of several theories of evolution', and drew the line clearly: theories which 'consider the spirit as emerging from the forces of living matter or as a mere epiphenomenon of this matter, are incompatible with the truth about man'. His address also says that 'the moment of transition to the spiritual cannot be the object of this kind of observation', which is a statement about the limits of method, not about biology. On polygenism, Humani Generis 37 states that the faithful 'cannot embrace that opinion which maintains that either after Adam there existed on this earth true men who did not take their origin through natural generation from him as from the first parent of all, or that Adam represents a certain number of first parents', on the ground that 'it is in no way apparent how such an opinion can be reconciled' with the Church's teaching on original sin as proceeding from a sin actually committed by an individual Adam and passed on through generation. That is a real restriction, and it is not a solemn definition; the honest description is that the encyclical's argument remains authoritative and the question has continued to be discussed. Finally, original sin itself: Trent defined that Adam's sin injured his posterity, that it is transmitted and not merely imitated, and that it is remitted by baptism; what Trent did not do is describe the mechanism, and the Catechism says so: 'the transmission of original sin is a mystery that we cannot fully understand' (CCC 404).
lessons.example: Sort six claims into four containers: defined, authoritative teaching that is not a definition, legitimate theological opinion, and error. Claim one: 'Each human soul is immediately created by God.' Container: authoritative teaching stated by an encyclical (Humani Generis 36) and repeated by John Paul II; it is the settled Catholic position, and it is not one of the solemn definitions of a general council, which matters if you are trying to describe precisely what kind of assent it asks. Claim two: 'The soul is transmitted by the parents along with the body.' Container: an opinion held by some early writers (traducianism) and never adopted by the Church; it conflicts with claim one as Pius XII stated it. Claim three: 'Adam and Eve are literary symbols for a population of early humans, so there was no single first human pair.' Container: error, in the specific form Humani Generis 37 addressed, because the encyclical grounds the transmission of original sin in a sin actually committed by an individual Adam; a student who wants to argue the point must argue with the text rather than around it, and must show how the doctrine of original sin survives the claim. Claim four: 'The human body may have developed through evolutionary processes.' Container: legitimate, explicitly permitted since Humani Generis and affirmed as 'more than a hypothesis' by John Paul II in 1996, who also insisted there are 'several theories of evolution' and that materialist readings are 'incompatible with the truth about man'. Claim five: 'Original sin is only a bad example set by our ancestors, which we now imitate.' Container: error, explicitly anathematised by Trent's fifth session: if anyone asserts that Adam injured 'himself alone, and not his posterity', or that he 'has only transfused death, and pains of the body, into the whole human race, but not sin also', let him be anathema. Claim six: 'The way original sin is passed on to each person can be explained as biological inheritance.' Container: not taught; the Catechism calls the transmission 'a mystery that we cannot fully understand' (CCC 404) while affirming that we are 'born afflicted' with it. The exercise is not about memorising labels; it is about noticing that claims one, four and six sound similar in casual speech and belong in three different containers.
lessons.question: A catechist says: 'Because the Church teaches that human beings evolved, and because Adam is therefore a symbol, we should read original sin as a description of social structures rather than of anything inherited.' Identify the two distinct errors in that sentence and the documents that rule them out.
lessons.answer: The first error is the inference from permitted evolution to a symbolic Adam: the Church permits the evolution of the human body while requiring that the soul is immediately created by God, and Humani Generis 37 states that the faithful cannot embrace the opinion that Adam 'represents a certain number of first parents', because 'it is in no way apparent' how that can be reconciled with original sin proceeding from a sin actually committed by an individual Adam. The second error is the reduction of original sin to social structure or bad example, which Trent's fifth session condemned when it anathematised the view that Adam injured himself alone and transmitted only death and bodily pains, 'but not sin also'.
lessons.distractor: Only the first is an error: original sin as a description of social sin is actually the Church's modern emphasis, and the Church has accepted that Adam was not a historical individual since the 1950 encyclical treated evolution as a serious hypothesis.
lessons.correction: The distractor gets the documents backwards on both points. Humani Generis 36-37 does not concede a symbolic Adam; it distinguishes the origin of the human body, about which discussion is permitted, from polygenism, about which it says the children of the Church 'by no means enjoy such liberty' and gives its reason. And original sin is not reducible to social sin: Trent's fifth session defines both that Adam's transgression injured his posterity and that what is passed on includes sin, not merely death and bodily suffering; the Catechism restates it as a sin 'with which we are all born afflicted, a sin which is the "death of the soul"' (CCC 403) and calls its transmission 'a mystery that we cannot fully understand' (CCC 404). Social sin is a real category in Catholic moral theology, but it describes structures and cultures; the doctrine of original sin describes a condition of each person from the beginning, antecedent to their own choices, which is exactly why infants are baptised for the remission of sins even though they have committed none. A student who answers 'only the first is an error' has accepted a popular re-description and attributed it to the Church. The correct answer distinguishes the permitted hypothesis (evolution of the body), the restricted hypothesis (polygenism, restricted by an authoritative encyclical argument rather than by a solemn definition), and the defined doctrine (the transmission of sin from Adam, its remission in baptism), and it can give the document for each.

depth.definitions: Image of God (imago Dei): the human person's likeness to God, located in a spiritual soul with intellect and will and fulfilled in relationship to God and neighbour; not, in Catholic teaching, reducible to any single faculty or to the species alone. Body-soul unity: the human person is one being, the soul being the substantial form of the body — a claim that rules out both a dualism that treats the body as a tool and a materialism that treats the mind as a by-product. Immediate creation of the soul: the teaching that each human soul is created directly by God rather than generated by the parents (Humani Generis 36). Traducianism: the rejected alternative, that the soul is transmitted with generation. Monogenism / polygenism: the monogenetic view holds that all humans descend from one original pair; polygenism holds that they descend from a population, and Humani Generis 37 judges that it is 'in no way apparent' how polygenism can be reconciled with the Church's doctrine of original sin. Original sin: the state of deprivation of original holiness and justice into which each person is born, consequent on the sin of Adam, distinct from personal sin and from concupiscence (the inclination to sin), though tied to it. Prerequisites: grace and justification (level 36); the person/nature distinction (lesson 72); the fact/interpretation tools of level 61-62.
depth.mechanism: Why does the Church keep the two questions — the origin of the body and the origin of the soul — apart? Because they have different sources of evidence and different kinds of authority. The bodily history of the human species is a matter for the natural sciences, whose methods cannot detect the presence of a spiritual principle (John Paul II's point that 'the moment of transition to the spiritual cannot be the object of this kind of observation'); the soul's creation is a matter of revelation and of the metaphysics that revelation requires, and no experimental result could confirm or refute it. This division of labour is what allowed Pius XII to permit evolutionary research while requiring a doctrine of the soul, and it is what makes the polygenism restriction so interesting: here the Church is not arguing about biology at all but about the coherence of a revealed doctrine. If original sin is a state transmitted from a single originating sin, then a theory that removes the single originating sin needs an account of how the doctrine survives; Humani Generis concludes that such an account was not then apparent, which is a claim about the state of the argument rather than a definition that closes the question forever. Note the asymmetries that a careful student should respect. Immediate creation of the soul is taught by an encyclical and by the Catechism's anthropology (CCC 366 uses the same language); traducianism has never been accepted. The restriction on polygenism is stated in an argument whose premises are doctrinal but whose conclusion is about apparent reconcilability. The doctrine of original sin's transmission is defined at Trent in the canons, while its mechanism is expressly left as a mystery (CCC 404). Where the Church has not settled a question — the precise biology of human origins, the moment and mode of the infusion of the soul, how concupiscence is related to the privation of grace in each person — the correct answer is that these are open, and arguments about them are theological and scientific, not confessional.
depth.secondExample: Take the pastoral question that keeps returning in catechism classes: what happens to infants who die without baptism? Three sources must be held together. Trent defined that original sin is real, transmitted and remitted by baptism, and that infants are baptised for the remission of sins. The Catechism, in the 1992 edition, does not mention limbo at all, and entrusts such children to the mercy of God. The International Theological Commission's 2007 study states explicitly that the theory of limbo — a state without the beatific vision but without punishment — was 'elaborated by theologians beginning in the Middle Ages' and 'never entered into the dogmatic definitions of the Magisterium', so that it 'remains therefore a possible theological hypothesis', and the study concludes that there are 'theological and liturgical reasons to hope' for these children.
